dct_description_sm: Arctic wildlife is influenced by multiple interactive stressors including rapid climate change impacting ice conditions and contaminant burdens. With increasing temperatures that reduce sea ice cover, migratory seabirds must adapt and alter their annual use of sea- and landscapes. With warming, contaminants increase or decrease, and with changing migration, wildlife may be exposed differentially to contaminants, which is also concerning for long-term country foods security. Since 2022, thick-billed murres (an Arctic seabird) breeding at Appatuurjuaq (Coats Island, Hudson Bay), were blood sampled, eggs collected, and outfitted with GLS geolocators which tracked their annual movements to identify and understand where and when seabirds are impacted by climate change and contaminants, and thus infer when, where, and how, sea ice conditions influence migration and contaminant impacts. Microplastics, plastics-related organophosate esters (OPEs) and UV-328 (ultra-violet stabilizer), per- and poly-fluorinated alkyl acids (PFAS), and mercury, were analyzed in the murres breeding at Appatuurjuaq and those overwintering near Nain, Nunatsiavut. Parental blood samples and their eggs provide spatial-temporal insights into contaminants accumulated during spring migration (eggs) and mid-breeding season (blood samples), while liver samples from overwintering, community-harvested murres identify contaminants accumulated during fall migration and early winter. Former Post-Doctoral Fellow and NSERC Banting Scholar, Dr. Anis Mdieu, (now IRD, France) continues collaborating with project members to analyze, interpret, and communicate results from our current (2023-2026) and previous (2019-2022) NCP research (M20); our first paper characterizes maternal transfer of PFAS, particularly long-chain PFCAs (Mdieu, A., Elliott, K.H., Letcher, R.J., Gousy-Leblanc, M., Fernie, K.J. 2026. Throwing off the long chains: maternal transfer of perfluoroalkyl acids increases with chain length in an Arctic seabird. Environmental Pollution 127979). Upcoming publications address maternal transfer of mercury, OPEs and UV-328, plus determine where and when murres accumulate measured pollutants during their annual movements and how this is influenced by sea ice conditions to inform long-term predictions about climate change and contaminants trends in Arctic seabirds and country foods security. We thank CIRNAC, ECCC, McGill University, Nunatsiavut Government, etc for funding and logistical support.
